title: Violence Against Migrants: The Hatred That Must Also Be Investigated
author: Diego Torres
content:
_This article by Diego Torres appears in the November 2026 issue of_ Let's
Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a magazine on migration
issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes.[Read and
download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

Violence against migrants is not new in U.S. history, but it has intensified
under the Trump administration, from his rhetoric to ICE operations and racial
profiling cases. In March 2026, a federal judge found “compelling and
troubling” evidence that immigration agents in Minnesota made arrests based on
people’s race or ethnicity.

We have already addressed the issue of violence in the United States, where
shootings and massacres are not uncommon. In 2025, the FBI received reports of
10,881 hate incidents, with 13,438 victims. In incidents motivated by a single
type of prejudice, more than half of the victims were targeted due to racial,
ethnic, or ancestry bias. These figures are alarming when we consider that
undocumented immigrants tend not to report crimes. Recent studies have found
that fear of deportation and the involvement of local police in immigration
enforcement reduce the willingness of immigrant communities to come forward.
This suggests that the problem may be far more serious than official
statistics indicate.

As I mentioned earlier, violence against migrants is not new, nor is the fear
many migrants have of reporting it. Years ago, the U visa was created as a
measure to address precisely this situation. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration
Services itself acknowledges that when Congress created this protection in
2000, it took into account that people without legal immigration status could
be especially vulnerable and that many avoided cooperating with authorities
for fear of deportation. The U visa sought to protect victims of certain
crimes and, at the same time, make it easier for them to report the crimes and
cooperate with investigations.

The option worked, but currently the number of applications far exceeds the
system's capacity. The law allows only 10,000 primary U visas to be granted
per year, and that limit has been reached every year since 2010. The process
can take years. Furthermore, filing an application does not guarantee
immediate protection from deportation: USCIS must first make a favorable
determination or place the applicant on a waiting list before they can receive
deferred action and employment authorization.

On the other hand, the fear of reporting that this measure seeks While the
problem has diminished, it has returned strongly when migrants observe local
police working in coordination with ICE. This is not merely a perception. The
federal 287(g) program allows state and local authorities to receive limited
powers to perform certain immigration functions under ICE supervision. A study
published in 2016 in American Economics… The review found that police
participation in immigration enforcement programs reduced the likelihood of
Hispanic victims reporting crimes, and as reports decreased, crimes against
this population increased. Migrants feel that going to the police could also
pose an immigration risk and therefore prefer not to report crimes.

As can be seen, if relatively common crimes go unreported and unaddressed, it
will be much harder to expect the government to acknowledge potential hate
crimes committed against migrants, even when these occur during operations
carried out by the authorities themselves. Cases of racial profiling have
already reached the courts. In Minnesota, a federal judge concluded that there
was evidence of arrests made solely based on race or ethnicity during
immigration operations.

The vulnerability of migrants is alarming, as is the indifference of the Trump
administration and the governments of the countries of origin. The number of
migrant deaths is significant, but it represents only the most publicized
aspect. Reports of excessive use of force, racial profiling, and other abuses
continue to surface. In March 2026, the United Nations Committee on the
Elimination of Racial Discrimination expressed its concern about reports of
violence and excessive use of force during immigration operations, as well as
the racial profiling of people perceived as migrants.

Abuses against migrants attempting to enter the United States had already been
reported during the Biden administration, but this history is rarely mentioned
today. Human Rights Watch documented cases in 2024 of Mexican asylum seekers
being blocked, mistreated, and returned to Mexico by border agents.

![Violence Against Migrants: The Hatred That Must Also Be
Investigated](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-02-body-p07.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

If we add to this the fact that figures like Gregory Bovino exist within the
Border Patrol, we can better understand what migrants have faced for decades.
Bovino became one of the most visible faces of this administration's
immigration operations. The Associated Press documented tactics that included
breaking vehicle windows, using chemical agents, and large-scale operations,
while his strategy of quick arrests, known as "turn and burn," generated
strong criticism during operations in Minnesota.

The midterm elections on November 3, 2026, will also determine the political
margin within which Trump can continue to push his agenda for the next two
years.

Trump has used immigrants to explain many of the nation's problems and has
repeatedly made accusations about the alleged illegal voting of non-citizens.
Some of these claims have not been substantiated. In July 2016, for example,
he claimed that thousands of undocumented immigrants had voted in New Jersey,
but the available data did not support that claim.

He even recently announced a $1 million reward. On October 26, Trump offered
that amount to anyone who provides information about voter fraud leading to an
arrest and conviction. The reward was not specifically announced for anyone
who proves that immigrants vote, although it comes amid a campaign in which
Trump has consistently insisted on linking immigration to alleged voter fraud.

This also forces us to remember what happened on January 6, 2021, when Trump
supporters stormed the Capitol while Congress was meeting to certify the
Electoral College votes from the 2020 presidential election.

If Trump's current political tactics fail, his opponents may consider it a
victory. But that doesn't necessarily mean a victory for migrants. The real
danger is that some of the anger that has been simmering for years will end up
being directed against a population that has been consistently portrayed as
responsible for problems that extend far beyond immigration.

MAGA supporters will have to face the election results and the rhetoric they
have heard for years. The risk that this hatred will once again manifest
itself in acts of violence should not be ignored, especially since a United
Nations body has already warned that the public criminalization of migrants
can contribute to discrimination and hate crimes.

That is why we must demand that all governments recognize not only the
importance of migrants, but something even more urgent: that they denounce
hate speech, investigate abuses committed against this population and, where
legal means exist, recognize and prosecute hate crimes committed against
migrants.
